text.p: Russia's reformist government and communist-dominated parliament gear up on Thursday for the third day of a stand-off over the economy while President Boris Yeltsin prepares for a summit with the Group of Seven leaders.
The State Duma lower house of parliament is due to discuss the government's draft of a new tax code which the cabinet considers vital to form a new-style 1998 budget.
Reform guru and First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais said the tax code might win initial parliamentary approval.
"We consider the Thursday vote to be decisive," Chubais said, promising that the code could be amended in the committee stage to meet deputies' concerns.
But the experience of the past two days indicated that the deputies were not in an agreeable mood.
On Tuesday they threw out a package of bills to cut or scrap most Soviet-era welfare benefits, which the cabinet says have become too heavy a burden for the new Russia.
On Wednesday, the Duma again stalled a government plan to cut spending, despite rumours circulated among deputies that Yeltsin's patience was running out.

"I hope that the government will offer a constructive decision which will keep the Duma happy, although some differences would have to be reviewed separately," Yuri Maslyukov, a senior communist in the Duma, told reporters.
The government, he said, had agreed to scale back the spending cuts to around 85 trillion roubles ($15 billion) from 108 trillion -- about a fifth of total spending.
"We have other views but I think finally the figure will be around 50 trillion," Maslyukov said, although it was not clear if the government side shared this view.
The dispute has dragged on for weeks and brought threats of a no-confidence vote in the government or dissolution of parliament.
In a new twist, rumours spread around the Duma on Wednesday that Yeltsin had summoned his advisers to help him make a crisis decision in connection with the stalled reforms.
The Kremlin denied the rumours, which followed hints from ministers that Yeltsin was prepared to disband parliament to persuade deputies to pass the bills before their summer recess starts next week.
On Thursday Yeltsin is expected to meet Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin who is returning from a three-week Black Sea holiday.

Yeltsin is also due to record a regular radio address to the nation and give an interview to journalists from Russia and the G7 countries -- the United States, Japan, France, Germany, Britain, Italy and Canada.
He leaves later in the day for the summit in Denver, where he is sure to press Russia's case for joining the G7, underlining Russia's economic progress since the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.
